operators.notes: Full sequential scan of orders table (15M rows). Read o_custkey (int32, raw) and o_comment (varlen).
Varlen string pattern match. ~0.5% of orders match the pattern and are excluded. Use strstr or two-needle search (find 'special' then check 'requests' after).

operators.description: Per-customer order count via direct array
operators.notes: c_custkey is dense PK [1..1500000]. Each thread maintains a thread-local int32 array of size 1.5M+1. For each surviving order row, increment array[o_custkey]. Array fits in ~6MB per thread.

operators.description: Sum per-thread direct arrays into global count array
operators.notes: Element-wise addition of thread-local arrays. Can parallelize the merge across array segments. Output: global_order_count[custkey] = total qualifying orders for that customer.

operators.description: Derive c_count for every customer (LEFT JOIN semantics)
operators.logic: Iterate all c_custkey values [1..1500000]. c_count = global_order_count[custkey] (0 if customer had no qualifying orders, which is the LEFT JOIN NULL→0 behavior of COUNT(o_orderkey)).
operators.notes: Dense PK means simple array iteration. No hash probe needed — just iterate the range. Customers with 0 orders naturally get c_count=0.
c_count range is [0..~42] for SF10. Use a small direct array of size 50. Single-threaded scan of 1.5M entries into 50-element array — trivially fast.
~43 distinct c_count values. Trivial sort on tiny result set.

parallel_phases: step1-2-3: parallel scan + filter + per-thread aggregation (main cost)
step4: parallel merge of thread-local arrays (segment-parallel)
step5-6-7: single-threaded (1.5M array scan + tiny agg + tiny sort)
parallelism.notes: 64 threads × 6MB = 384MB for thread-local arrays. Fits easily in 376GB. Steps 5-7 operate on small data and run single-threaded to avoid synchronization overhead.
